title: Contrasting Fire‐Driven Erosion Processes Mobilise Distinct Organic Carbon Pools in Forest Landscapes
content:
Fire-driven erosion mobilises distinct organic carbon pools from forest landscapes. Following a wildfire in southeastern Australia, hillslope erosion exported recent ash-derived carbon, while debris flows mobilised older, chemically recalcitrant carbon. Combined post-fire carbon export increased 71-fold relative to unburned conditions, highlighting the need to represent both pathways in carbon budgets.


ABSTRACT

Wildfires can substantially alter organic carbon (C) cycling in forest ecosystems beyond immediate emissions from fuel combustion. Among these post-fire effects, lateral C mobilisation by water erosion is an important but poorly quantified flux, rarely incorporated into fire-related C budgets. Here, we quantified and characterised C mobilised by hillslope erosion and channel erosion by debris flows in highly fire-prone eucalypt forests in southeastern Australia. We monitored suspended and bedload C export from headwater catchments across fire severities until erosion returned to background levels, quantified C mobilisation from colluvium by debris flows, characterised C chemical recalcitrance in ash, soils, eroded sediments and colluvium, and constrained colluvial C age using radiocarbon measurements. We then upscaled these fluxes to the area affected by the 2009 Beechworth Fire. Over the three-year post-fire perturbation period, hillslope and channel erosion mobilised 15,866 t C (0.78 t C ha−1). Hillslope erosion accounted for 91% of this landscape-scale flux, compared with 9% from debris flows. The two processes mobilised contrasting C pools. Hillslope C export was dominated by young wildfire ash derived from incompletely combusted vegetation and the surface organic soil horizon. In contrast, debris flows generated substantial localised C pulses by eroding deeper colluvial deposits, with 2%–20% of mobilised C older than 6000 years. Chemically recalcitrant and highly recalcitrant forms accounted for 47%–60% of C in fire-affected hillslope sediments and 43%–74% in colluvium, highlighting the potential importance of these lateral fluxes for long-term C dynamics. Post-fire erosion mobilised C equivalent to only approximately 4% of direct fire C emissions, but the C mobilised during the three-year post-fire period was equivalent to approximately 210 years of background (unburnt) erosion. Thus, lateral erosion represents an additional and compositionally distinct pathway of fire-driven C redistribution that should be considered in fire-prone forest C budgets.
